definition.text: Any economic theory that treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem it sits within.

facts.text: It usually takes a holistic approach, mixing economic ideas with other subjects depending on the theorist.
Some economists treat it as a branch of established schools, for example classical economics with the old factor 'land' widened into natural capital.
UNEP's growing commitment to natural capital and full cost accounting under the 'green economy' banner could blur the lines between schools.

definition.text: Indicators built to measure how green an economy is, from human ecological impact to efficiency and green investment flows.

facts.text: Ordinary economic output and progress are measured with economic index indicators; green indices arose to capture human ecological impact as well.
The Global Green Economy Index measures green economic performance and perceptions of it in 130 countries along four dimensions.
Ecological footprint measurements are another standard used by municipal governments to gauge human impact.

title: Degrowth

definition.text: An academic and social movement, mainly in Europe, that calls for planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption to tackle social and ecological crises.

facts.text: Common policy goals include shrinking humanity's environmental impact, redistributing income and wealth within and between countries, and moving from materialistic values toward a convivial, participatory society.
It rejects growth in GDP as a measure of human and economic development, arguing that capitalism's focus on growth causes wide ecological damage and is not needed to raise living standards.
Degrowth writers argue that absolute decoupling of GDP from resource use and emissions is only possible for short periods, in specific places, or with small mitigation rates.
It warns that efficiency technologies can trigger the rebound effect, also called the Jevons paradox, cancelling out expected resource savings.
The movement names economist Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as its main intellectual inspiration; the French term décroissance was used for a 1979 translation of his essays.
The first international degrowth conference was held in Paris in 2008.
Critics call it vague, say it ignores rebound effects and lacks political support, and argue environmental taxes or tradable permits work much better.
Critics also note that far-reaching degrowth scenarios are projected to raise extreme poverty.

contested_note: Supporters say degrowth would improve living standards and protect ecosystems, while critics argue it is vague, politically unpopular and likely to raise poverty.

definition.text: The concrete measures degrowth writers propose for shrinking production and consumption fairly.

facts.text: A 2022 survey of degrowth literature from 2005 to 2020 found 530 specific policy proposals.

The ten most cited were universal basic income, shorter working time, job guarantees with a living wage, maximum income caps, declining caps on resource use and emissions, not-for-profit cooperatives, deliberative forums, reclaiming the commons, ecovillages and housing cooperatives.
In a Swedish survey, reduced working hours got about 50% support, a wealth tax 40%, a meat tax 30%, a maximum income 25% and a basic income 15%.

title: Growth versus environment debate

definition.text: The dispute over whether economic growth can be made compatible with environmental sustainability, with positions ranging from green growth through agrowth to degrowth.

facts.text: Green growth holds growth and sustainability compatible; agrowth is agnostic about growth and focuses on cutting environmental harm with effective instruments whether the economy grows or shrinks.
In a survey of academics publishing on the topic, under 1% favoured growth at all costs, 42% green growth, 31% agrowth and 17% degrowth.
Another survey of nearly 800 climate policy researchers found 28% support degrowth.
Critics of green growth point instead to frameworks such as the circular economy, steady-state economy, degrowth and doughnut economics.
A 2020 paper argued that changing economic paradigms is essential to prevent environmental destruction, listing options from reformist agrowth to radical degrowth, eco-socialism and eco-anarchism.

contested_note: Researchers are split on whether growth can continue while environmental pressures fall fast enough.
notes: No own article; passes curriculum test 5 (discussed on Degrowth, Green economy, Agrowth and Green growth pages).

title: Doughnut economics

definition.text: A doughnut-shaped picture of sustainable development that joins planetary boundaries (an outer ecological ceiling) with a social foundation of basic human needs (an inner ring).

facts.text: The hole in the middle shows people lacking life's essentials such as healthcare and education; the outer crust shows the ecological ceilings that must not be overshot.
Economist Kate Raworth developed it in a 2012 Oxfam paper and expanded it in her 2017 book Doughnut Economics.
An economy counts as prosperous when all twelve social foundations are met without overshooting any of the nine ecological ceilings, leaving a 'safe and just space for humanity'.
The social foundations draw on the UN Sustainable Development Goals; the ecological ceilings come from the planetary boundaries of Rockström and Steffen's group.
A 2018 study of 150 countries found none that met its citizens' basic needs while keeping resource use at a globally sustainable level.
Raworth says significant GDP growth is still needed for low- and middle-income countries to reach the social foundation.
Critics say it lacks empirical support; one formal test found higher economic freedom linked with less imbalance, not more.
Branko Milanović notes that bringing everyone to rich countries' median income would require world GDP to triple, which the model does not address.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether the model has empirical support and whether it fairly represents mainstream economics.

title: Eco-economic decoupling

definition.text: The idea that an economy could grow without a matching rise in pressure on the environment.

facts.text: In many economies rising production (GDP) increases environmental pressure; a decoupled economy would keep growing while using less water, fossil fuel and other resources.
It is often measured by the emission intensity of economic output, meaning pollution per unit of GDP.
In 2002 the OECD defined decoupling as breaking the link between 'environmental bads' and 'economic goods'.
Where decoupling has occurred, one proposed explanation is the shift to a service economy; the environmental Kuznets curve is a proposed model of it.

The UNEP International Resource Panel warned in 2011 that without decoupling humanity could use 140 billion tons of minerals, ores, fossil fuels and biomass a year by 2050, three times the then-current rate.
Its 2016 report found global material productivity had declined since about 2000, so the world economy needed more materials per unit of GDP, the opposite sometimes called overcoupling.
Proposed technologies to speed decoupling include energy-saving, metal- and mineral-saving, and freshwater- and biotic-resource-saving technologies.

contested_note: Whether, how far and how fast growth can be decoupled from environmental pressure is widely debated.

definition.text: Relative decoupling means environmental impact per unit of output falls while total impact may still rise; absolute decoupling means total impact falls while output grows.

facts.text: For absolute decoupling, resource efficiency must rise at least as fast as economic output and keep improving as the economy grows.
Under relative decoupling total environmental impacts still increase, only more slowly than GDP.
Tim Jackson found much evidence of relative decoupling in the global economy but said evidence for absolute decoupling is harder to find.
Between 1990 and 2015 carbon intensity per dollar of GDP fell 0.6% a year while population and income per person each grew 1.3% a year, so emissions rose about 2% a year.
Herman Daly noted that a dollar of GNP in 1969 used half the materials of a dollar in 1900, yet total material consumption rose 400 percent.

title: Five axes of decoupling
article: Eco-economic decoupling#Five axes to assess decoupling

definition.text: A set of at least five dimensions for judging whether a claimed case of decoupling is real and enough.

facts.text: Overall decoupling covers all environmental indicators, partial decoupling only some, which matters when cutting emissions raises, say, mining.
Local decoupling may simply move environmental stress to other countries by outsourcing production, unlike global decoupling.
Decoupling can be temporary if growth and pressures re-couple later; to be sufficient it must be large and fast enough to stay clear of critical tipping points.

definition.text: Resource decoupling cuts the resources used per unit of economic activity; impact decoupling cuts the environmental harm caused while output grows.

facts.text: Resource decoupling is also called dematerialization: using less material, energy, water and land for the same economic activity.
The impacts targeted by impact decoupling arise from extracting resources.

title: Decoupling evidence debate
article: Eco-economic decoupling#Lack of evidence for decoupling

definition.text: The dispute over whether growth has been, or can be, decoupled from environmental pressure fast enough to avoid serious damage.

facts.text: A 2020 study found no evidence of economy-wide decoupling nationally or internationally, and studies found absolute decoupling rare.
Critics say there is no evidence of decoupling near the needed scale and that a sufficiency approach must complement efficiency.
Hickel and Kallis's models assume carbon intensity falls at most 4% a year, which makes 1.5 °C impossible and 2 °C reachable only if rich economies shrink by over 90%.
Rikard Warlenius replies that absolute decoupling faster than that 4% threshold has already happened and stronger policies could push it higher.
He also argues growth is better placed than degrowth to fund the deep, costly transitions the IPCC describes.

contested_note: Degrowth scholars see no evidence of sufficient decoupling, while others point to cases of fast absolute decoupling and argue stronger policy could achieve more.

title: Green growth

definition.text: Paths of economic growth that are environmentally sustainable, a term used in economic theory and policymaking.

facts.text: It assumes growth can continue while environmental harms such as climate change fall, which requires decoupling growth from resource use and environmental impact.
The term was coined in 2005 by Rae Kwon Chung of UNESCAP and first emerged at a ministerial conference in Seoul.
The OECD published a Green Growth Strategy in 2011, and in 2012 the World Bank, UNEP, OECD and GGGI launched the Green Growth Knowledge Platform.
The ILO estimates a shift to a greener economy could create 24 million new jobs worldwide by 2030 if environmental policies are in place.

Claims of decoupling based on domestic material consumption ignore resource use shifted along global supply chains; the material footprint, which counts it, suggests resource use may grow about as fast as GDP.
One analysis found 92% of global GDP is in economies that have decoupled relatively or absolutely, and countries with over 46% of global GDP achieved absolute decoupling between 2015 and 2023.
A 2020 review of 835 papers concluded that observed decoupling rates cannot deliver large, rapid absolute cuts, so decoupling needs sufficiency strategies and strict reduction targets alongside it.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether observed decoupling is fast and large enough for green growth to meet environmental targets.

definition.text: The barriers that may make green growth wishful thinking, as listed by the European Environmental Bureau.

facts.text: The more natural resources are needed, the more expensive they become to extract.
Efficiency gains are often accompanied by the same or higher consumption of a good, and every technological fix brings its own environmental side effects.
The service economy rests on the material economy, so it adds a footprint rather than replacing it.
Apparent decoupling often comes from shifting environmental impact from high-consumption to low-consumption countries.

title: The Limits to Growth

definition.text: A 1972 report that used computer simulation to explore what happens when the economy and population grow exponentially on a planet with finite resources.

facts.text: Commissioned by the Club of Rome, it was written by Donella Meadows, Dennis Meadows, Jørgen Randers and William Behrens III for a team of 17 researchers.
It used the World3 computer model, built on Jay Forrester's work at MIT, to simulate interactions between Earth and human systems.
Two of its scenarios showed 'overshoot and collapse' of the global system by the mid to late 21st century, while a third produced a 'stabilized world'.

It concluded that if growth trends continued unchanged, limits would be reached within a hundred years, most likely with a sudden decline in population and industrial capacity, but that a stable, sustainable equilibrium was possible.
Critics called it 'Garbage In, Garbage Out', saying it gave too little weight to technological progress; price predictions based on scarcity did not come true.
About 30 million copies have been sold in 30 languages, and it influenced environmental reforms for decades.
Updates followed in 1992 (Beyond the Limits), 2004 (the 30-Year Update) and 2022 (Limits and Beyond).

contested_note: Critics called its models simplistic and too pessimistic about technology, while later comparisons with data have found reality tracking its business-as-usual run.
distinct_from: Limits to Growth compared with data

title: Exponential reserve index
article: The Limits to Growth#Exponential reserve index

definition.text: A way of estimating how long a resource will last when yearly use keeps growing, instead of simply dividing reserves by current use.

facts.text: In 1972 chromium reserves were 775 million metric tons with 1.85 million mined a year, a static index of 418 years.
With use growing 2.6% a year, the same reserves would last about 95 years.
The general formula is y = ln(rs + 1)/r, where r is the growth rate and s the static reserve (reserves divided by annual consumption).
Though the indexes were widely read as dates when the world would 'run out', Ugo Bardi argued the book never presented them as predictions.

distinct_from: Limits to Growth compared with data

title: Bariloche Model
article: The Limits to Growth#Latin American World Model (Bariloche Model)

definition.text: A world model built by Latin American scientists in answer to The Limits to Growth, arguing that the real limits to development were social and political, not physical.

facts.text: Researchers critiqued the MIT World3 model for reflecting the developed world's concerns while ignoring the realities of the Global South.
Published in English in 1976, it challenged the premise that population growth and resource depletion must lead to global collapse.

distinct_from: Limits to Growth compared with data

title: Limits to Growth compared with data
article: The Limits to Growth#Comparisons and updated models

definition.text: Later studies that check The Limits to Growth scenarios against what actually happened.

facts.text: In 2008 Graham Turner at CSIRO found thirty years of industrial production, food production and pollution data matched the book's 'business as usual' scenario, which leads to collapse in the 21st century.
A 2020 study by Gaya Herrington found data broadly consistent with the 1972 projections, with growth peaking and then declining rapidly by around 2040 unless resource use changes.
A 2023 recalibration of World3 with data up to 2022 showed the same overshoot-and-collapse pattern, with peaks raised and moved a few years later.
Brian Hayes called the model 'more a polemical tool than a scientific instrument'.

contested_note: Some analysts find data tracking the collapse scenario, while others say the model is a polemical tool, not a predictor.

definition.text: An umbrella term for economic, ecological and political views that accept endless economic growth cannot last on a finite planet.

facts.text: It moves the economy's main goal from GDP growth to well-being, arguing prosperity is possible beyond growth.
Some scholars split it into degrowth and agrowth; others include doughnut and wellbeing economics and steady-state economics.
Typical post-growth policies are shorter working time, universal basic income, wealth taxes, carbon taxes with strong redistribution, and universal basic services.
Post-growth puts sustainability and social justice ahead of growth, while degrowth goes further and calls for deliberately shrinking economic activity.
A 2023 study of nearly 800 climate policy researchers found 73% support post-growth (45% agrowth and 28% degrowth).

title: Rebound effect

definition.text: The loss of part of the expected savings from a more efficient technology, because people and the economy respond by using more.

facts.text: It is expressed as the share of the expected saving that is lost: if a 5% gain in fuel efficiency cuts fuel use by only 2%, the rebound is 60%.
The 'missing' saving may go into driving faster or further than before.
Most economists agree it exists but disagree about how large and important it is.
It was first described by William Stanley Jevons in his 1865 book The Coal Question, which observed that a more efficient steam engine opened many new uses for coal.
Though studied mostly for energy, the idea applies to any natural resource or input, including labour.
Studies of home heating, cooling and personal transport often find rebounds of 20–50%.
Direct rebounds tend to be higher in low-income households, which have been cutting back on heating because of its cost.

contested_note: Researchers agree the rebound effect exists but disagree about its size and importance for policy.

definition.text: The three ways the economy can take back efficiency savings: the direct, indirect and economy-wide rebound effects.

facts.text: Direct rebound: a good is used more because it has become cheaper to use, as when cheaper driving leads to more driving.
Indirect rebound: the money saved is spent on other goods and services, such as savings from an efficient cooling system spent on a luxury.
Economy-wide rebound: cheaper services lower other prices, open new production possibilities and speed up economic growth.
Indirect effects from household conservation can range from 10% to 200% depending on the scenario.
Even if direct and indirect rebounds add up to less than 100%, faster growth from efficiency can still raise the economy's total resource use.

title: Time rebound effect
article: Rebound effect (conservation)#Rebounds with respect to time

definition.text: Extra resource use that follows when a technology saves people time, which they then spend on more of the service or other activities.

facts.text: Faster transport lowers the real cost of commuting but encourages longer commutes, which raise energy use.
Its scale is almost impossible to measure because people value time subjectively.

definition.text: Measures that keep efficiency gains from being eaten up by extra use, usually by holding the cost of use steady or higher.

facts.text: Wackernagel and Rees suggested that cost savings from efficiency be 'taxed away' and preferably reinvested in restoring natural capital.
Tools include green taxes, cap and trade, higher fuel taxes, or targeting the yearly energy use of a system rather than device efficiency.
Fuel use falls unambiguously if efficiency gains are paired with a measure such as a fuel tax that keeps fuel costs the same or higher.

title: Kuznets curve

definition.text: Simon Kuznets's hypothesis that, as an economy develops, market forces first raise and then lower economic inequality, tracing an inverted U.

facts.text: One explanation is that early industrialization draws cheap rural labour to cities, holding wages down while owners profit, before democratization and the welfare state spread the gains.
The hypothesis remains highly contested, with no consensus about its validity.
Inequality has risen in most developed countries since the 1960s, so the data no longer show the curve.
Kuznets himself warned the data were fragile and covered a very limited period, but other economists raised the curve 'to the level of law'.
The East Asian miracle, rapid growth in eight East Asian economies between 1965 and 1990 with falling poverty, has been used to challenge it.

contested_note: Economists have no consensus that inequality really rises then falls with development.

title: Environmental Kuznets curve

definition.text: The hypothesis that environmental damage gets worse as an economy grows until average income reaches a certain level, after which it improves.

facts.text: There is considerable evidence of the inverted-U pattern for some indicators such as water and air pollution, with pollutants like sulfur dioxide, lead and DDT cited.
Between 1970 and 2006 US real GDP grew 195% while sulfur dioxide emissions fell from 31 million tons to 15 million and lead emissions fell by more than 98%.
Net deforestation has ceased among countries with per capita GDP of at least $4,600, though rich countries may be 'exporting' deforestation.
Energy, land and resource use may not fall with rising income, and total energy use and many greenhouse gas emissions still rise in most developed countries.
Carbon may not follow the curve because, unlike local pollutants such as lead, cutting CO2 brings little local benefit, a tragedy of the commons.
Some researchers find an 'N' shape, with pollution rising again as income keeps growing, or argue pollution is simply exported to poorer countries.
It is a proposed model for eco-economic decoupling.

contested_note: Evidence supports the curve for some local pollutants, but its application to carbon, resource use and biodiversity is disputed.

title: Material Kuznets curve
article: Kuznets curve#Kuznets curves for steel and other metals

definition.text: The finding that a country's use of steel and other metals rises and then falls over its course of development, like a Kuznets curve.

facts.text: Steel production follows a Kuznets-type curve in economies including the United States, Japan, South Korea and China.
The terms 'Kuznets Curve for Steel' and 'Metal intensity Kuznets Curve' were first used by Huw McKay in 2008.

definition.text: The policy stance of being indifferent to GDP growth when designing policies for economic and social progress.

facts.text: Its reasoning is that GDP growth does not correlate closely with real progress.
In environmental policy it is opposed to both green growth and degrowth.
Economist Jeroen van den Bergh argues policy should neither chase nor avoid growth but directly use effective tools such as environmental taxes or emission rights to price externalities.
Whether the economy then grows, stagnates or shrinks is of secondary importance.

definition.text: An environmental philosophy that relies on advanced technology, social innovation, eco-innovation and sustainable design to solve environmental problems.

facts.text: It contrasts with environmentalism that calls for less consumption or simpler lifestyles.
Writer Alex Steffen coined the term in 2003.
Its core idea is that good communities, new technologies and sustainable living can raise quality of life while ecological footprints shrink.
Dark greens cite the Jevons paradox to argue technological approaches have limited benefits.

title: Dark, light and bright greens
article: Bright green environmentalism#Dark greens, light greens and bright greens

definition.text: Alex Steffen's three-way split of environmentalists into dark, light and bright greens.

facts.text: Light greens treat protecting the environment mainly as a personal responsibility and lifestyle choice.
Dark greens see environmental problems as built into industrial, capitalist civilization and its emphasis on growth, and seek radical change.
Bright greens also want radical change but believe better design, new technology and social innovation are the way to get it.

definition.text: In political and degrowth thought, the ability of people to act creatively and independently with others and their environment to meet their own needs.

facts.text: Ivan Illich introduced this meaning in his 1973 book Tools for Conviviality, as the opposite of industrial productivity that turns people into 'mere consumers'.
Convivial tools, such as most hand tools, bicycles and telephones, extend people's autonomy, unlike open-pit mines or road networks.
It is a core concept of degrowth, and degrowth writers generally accept that technologies suited to a degrowth society must be convivial.
Convivial tools resemble the 'intermediate technology' of E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful.

title: Degrowth in the Global South

definition.text: The study of whether and how degrowth ideas apply to the countries of the Global South.

facts.text: Applying degrowth there is debated, since many Southern countries still have unmet basic needs and may need some material growth.
Many of degrowth's roots lie in Southern traditions such as Buen Vivir in the Andes and Ubuntu in Southern Africa.
Some frame Northern degrowth as decolonization: shrinking the North's footprint to leave room for the South, linked to the idea of ecological debt.
Critics warn Northern degrowth could destabilize export-dependent Southern economies.

contested_note: Scholars disagree on whether degrowth suits countries that still need growth to meet basic needs.

definition.text: A strategy of shrinking a society's environmental footprint by moderating its demand for energy, carbon and material-based goods and services.

facts.text: As a goal, it means everyone living a good life within planetary boundaries; as a strategy, it means limiting consumption and production without threatening basic human needs.
The IPCC defines it as policies and daily practices that avoid demand for energy, materials, land and water while providing wellbeing for all within planetary boundaries.
Thomas Princen popularised the term in his 2005 book The Logic of Sufficiency.
Its proponents argue that because of efficiency's limits and rebound effects, demand cannot fall enough unless the energy services societies rely on are themselves questioned.
Together with efficiency and consistency it is one of the fundamental sustainability strategies.
A German study found sufficiency measures could theoretically cut household energy use by 70%.
Wolfgang Sachs's 'Four D's' of sufficiency include decelerating, decentralizing and decommercializing.
Critics share their objection to degrowth: it could hurt growth and raise unemployment; sufficiency savings can also cause indirect rebound effects.

title: Ecological overshoot

definition.text: What happens when the demands placed on an ecosystem exceed its ability to regenerate.

facts.text: Global overshoot occurs when humanity demands more than Earth's biosphere can renew.
William R. Catton Jr.'s 1980 book Overshoot is credited with the term's scientific use for humanity's global impact.
Footprint accounts show humanity has exceeded Earth's regenerative capacity every year since 1970.
A country with a footprint smaller than its biocapacity has an ecological reserve; over 85% of the world's people live in countries in overshoot.
Earth Overshoot Day marks the date each year when humanity's resource use exceeds what Earth can regenerate that year.
Global Footprint Network estimated that as of 2022 humanity used natural capital 71% faster than Earth renews it.
Persistent overshoot would suggest continued ecological deterioration and a possibly permanent fall in Earth's carrying capacity for people.
WWF's Living Planet Report 2022 recorded a 69% decline in vertebrate populations since 1970 and linked it to humanity exceeding global biocapacity.

notes: Also drafted in footprints-and-indicators with the same article; the coordinator should keep one copy (this is a seed of growth-decoupling-and-limits).; Ecological overshoot is a seed of growth-decoupling-and-limits; drafted here from footprint sentences. Fold with that chapter's entry at selection.

title: Ecomodernism

definition.text: An environmental philosophy holding that technology can protect nature and improve human wellbeing by decoupling economic growth from environmental impact.

facts.text: It accepts replacing natural ecosystem services with energy, technology and synthetic solutions when these reduce environmental impact.
A key aim is to use technology to intensify human activity, such as high-yield farming and dense cities, so as to leave more room for wild nature.
In April 2015, 18 self-described ecomodernists published An Ecomodernist Manifesto.
It sets itself apart from ecological economics, degrowth, population reduction and the 'soft energy' path.
Eighteen ecological economists replied with 'A Degrowth Response to an Ecomodernist Manifesto', and critics say it ignores mass extinction and the unequal sides of technological modernisation.

contested_note: Degrowth and steady-state economists, among others, reject ecomodernism's confidence that technology can decouple growth from nature.

definition.text: The amount of a resource a country can use without endangering its continued availability, assuming everyone in the world has an equal share.

facts.text: It requires knowing the maximum sustainable use of every resource, set by sustainable yield or by the environment's capacity to absorb waste, both hard to estimate.
Each resource has its own units, so environmental spaces cannot be added into one national total.
Friends of the Earth Europe promoted it in the mid-1990s, but it has largely been superseded by the ecological footprint, which converts all resource use into land area.

title: Factor 10

definition.text: A policy goal of a tenfold cut in resource use per unit of output, so that economies stay within the planet's carrying capacity.

facts.text: Friedrich Schmidt-Bleek of the Wuppertal Institute first proposed Factor 10 and dematerialization in the early 1990s.
It grew from Factor 4, which aims to cut resource and energy use by 75% by doubling output while halving inputs.
It responds to a UNEP call for a tenfold cut in industrialized countries' resource use so enough is left for developing countries.
Businesses and governments have pursued it through eco-efficiency, design for environment and environmental taxes.

notes: Overlaps the 'Factor X' entry drafted in footprints-and-indicators (article Material input per unit of service#Factor X concept); the coordinator may merge.

definition.text: A movement calling for public policy that tackles climate change while also creating jobs, supporting economic growth and reducing inequality.

facts.text: It draws on the idea that the climate crisis needs a large initiative like Roosevelt's New Deal.
On 22 October 2008 UNEP launched a Global Green New Deal in response to the Great Recession, aiming to create green jobs, boost the world economy and curb climate change.
In the UK, the Green New Deal Group and New Economics Foundation proposed one as a way out of the Great Recession.
The 2019 US resolution by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ed Markey called for moving to 100% renewable, zero-emission energy within 10 years.
Environmental justice is an explicit part of it, focusing on communities of color, Indigenous peoples and low-income communities.
The European Commission's 2019 European Green Deal is less ambitious on timing, aiming for carbon neutrality in 2050.
Many supporters of its goals doubt the feasibility of parts of it; one former US science adviser called the 2030 goal too optimistic.

title: Growth imperative

definition.text: The idea that an economy may be forced to grow, because firms, households or governments face serious harm without growth.

facts.text: At the micro level, it means firms or households must raise revenue or consumption to protect their income.
At the macro level, a political growth imperative exists if growth is needed to avoid economic and social instability, pushing goals such as climate mitigation below growth.
Marxist theory holds that competition forces firms to 'grow or die'; critics reply that a firm can stay profitable without growth by paying profits out as dividends.
Unemployment from technical progress without growth (Okun's law) is a central argument for the political imperative.
Proposed ways out include resource taxes, shorter working time, and fairer income distribution such as basic income.
Whether it is a meaningful concept at all, and which mechanism causes it, is disputed, including within the post-growth movement.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether any real growth imperative exists and what would cause it.

title: Monetary growth imperative
article: Growth imperative#Monetary system and the role of positive interest rates

definition.text: The claim that money created as interest-bearing debt forces the economy to keep growing.

facts.text: Hans Christoph Binswanger estimated a minimum necessary growth rate of 1.8%, Mathias Binswanger one of 0.45%.
Critics using stock-flow consistent models show repaid interest flows back into the economy, so debt can be serviced without growth if money is not hoarded.
On this view, the savings rate rather than the interest rate decides whether a non-growing economy is stable.

contested_note: Some authors find a growth imperative in interest-bearing money, while model-based critics say none arises from debt-based money as such.

title: Human overpopulation

definition.text: The idea that human populations may grow too large to be supported by their environment or resources over the long term.

facts.text: Since 1804 world population has grown from 1 billion to 8 billion thanks to medical advances and higher farm productivity.
Annual population growth peaked at 2.1% in 1968 and has since dropped to 1.1%; the UN projects a peak of about 10.4 billion in the 2080s.
The IPCC found GDP per person and population growth were the strongest drivers of fossil CO2 emissions in 2010–2019, raising emissions about 2.3% and 1.2% a year respectively.
Proponents say overpopulation, population growth and overconsumption together are the main drivers of human-caused environmental problems such as climate change.
Thomas Malthus predicted in the early 19th century that population would outgrow the resources a finite amount of land can supply.
Poverty and infant mortality have declined over 200 years of population growth, and the predicted 'population explosion' did not happen as growth slowed.
Critics call the concept racist because population control often targets the Global South rather than overconsumption in the Global North.

contested_note: Whether overpopulation is a real cause of environmental problems, rather than consumption or technology, is strongly disputed.

definition.text: Proposals to stabilize and then gradually reduce human numbers as a response to overpopulation.

facts.text: Suggested approaches include better access to contraception and sex education, and lower infant mortality so parents need fewer children.
Educating and empowering women and giving access to family planning have a demonstrated effect in lowering birthrates.
Nearly 40% of pregnancies worldwide are unintended, some 80 million a year.
Coercive measures such as China's one-child policy and compulsory sterilization have drawn strong criticism.

title: I = PAT

definition.text: A formula stating that human impact on the environment (I) is the product of population (P), affluence (A) and technology (T).

facts.text: It was developed in 1970 during a debate between Barry Commoner, Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren; Commoner blamed production technology, Ehrlich and Holdren stressed population growth.
Affluence is average consumption per person, often proxied by GDP per capita; technology measures how resource-intensive that affluence is, such as emissions per unit of GDP.
Impact can be measured in global hectares with ecological footprint analysis; if it exceeds carrying capacity the system is in overshoot.
The Kaya identity is a similar formula applied specifically to carbon dioxide emissions.
Critics say P, A and T are not independent: halving T may not halve impact if cheaper use stimulates more consumption, the rebound effect.
It is also faulted for ignoring political context and for blaming the global poor.
It underpins the World3 simulation model.

contested_note: Environmentalists debate whether impact can be written as a simple product of independent factors and which factors matter most.

title: Khazzoom–Brookes postulate

definition.text: The claim that energy-efficiency improvements that make sense for individual users lead to higher total energy use across the economy.

facts.text: Economists Daniel Khazzoom and Leonard Brookes put forward the idea independently in the 1980s; Harry Saunders named it in 1992 and showed it holds in neoclassical growth theory under many assumptions.
Efficiency raises energy use by making energy cheaper, by speeding economic growth, and by unlocking other activities that a scarce resource had held back.
After the 1973 and 1979 oil crises cars became more fuel-efficient on average, yet total consumption kept rising.
It is a modern version of the Jevons paradox.

contested_note: Economists debate whether the postulate is correct and how much it matters for energy policy.

definition.text: Using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused.

facts.text: Applied to natural resources harmed by use, it means the same as overexploitation.
It is driven by consumerism, planned obsolescence, economic materialism and other unsustainable business models, and contrasts with sustainable consumption.
Long-term overconsumption in a region can shrink natural resources and degrade the environment.
Excessive consumption beyond the environment's long-term carrying capacity causes ecological overshoot, resource depletion and poorer ecosystem health.
In 2010 the International Resource Panel found household consumption for mobility, shelter, food and energy-using products causes most of the life-cycle impacts of consumption.
Growing economies can drive it: China's consumption surpassed the biocapacity of its natural resources by 1983.
Movements against it include anti-consumerism, degrowth, frugality, downshifting, simple living and minimalism, many aiming at a steady-state economy.
The term is controversial and lacks a single agreed definition.

definition.text: The argument that the richest consumers drive a disproportionate share of overconsumption and its environmental harm.

facts.text: A 2020 Oxfam-SEI report found the top 10% of earners cause over half of global carbon emissions, and the richest 1% emit more than double the poorest 50% combined.
The 2020 'Scientists' warning on affluence' linked growth-driven economies since World War II to rising inequality, resource use and environmental pressure.
Proposed responses include progressive taxes on high-carbon activities, curbing luxury emissions and moving priorities from GDP growth to sustainability.

definition.text: The state in which a species' population is larger than the carrying capacity of its environment.

facts.text: It can follow higher birth rates, lower death rates, less predation or large migrations, leaving animals competing for food, space and resources.
Judgements of overpopulation always mix facts and values; animals are often called overpopulated when they cause harm people care about.
In ecology the concept is used mainly in wildlife management, for example for the worldwide rise in deer numbers.
Predator–prey models of population cycles are also used to set the maximum sustainable yield of fisheries.

title: Planned obsolescence

definition.text: Designing a product with an artificially short useful life or a deliberately weak design so that it stops working, or looks out of date, after a set time.

facts.text: The aim is to boost long-term sales by shortening the time between repeat purchases, the 'replacement cycle'.
It works best when a producer has at least an oligopoly, and relies on the buyer not knowing how long the product was designed to last.
Product lifespans tend to rise as markets become more competitive, as when longer-lasting Japanese cars pushed American carmakers to build more durable vehicles.
In the 1920s General Motors' Alfred P. Sloan Jr. introduced yearly model changes to keep car sales up in a saturated market.
In 2015 France set fines of up to €300,000 and up to two years in jail for planning product failure, the first legislature to recognize the practice.
In the US it is being tackled through state right-to-repair laws.
Supporters such as Philip Kotler see it as competition and technology at work, while critics such as Vance Packard call it wasteful and exploitative.

contested_note: Supporters see shortened replacement cycles as a product of competition and innovation, critics as waste and exploitation of customers.

definition.text: The different ways products are made to become obsolete, from built-in short lifetimes to deliberate disabling.

facts.text: Contrived durability shortens a product's life before release by designing it to wear out quickly, for example with inferior materials in critical parts.
Prevention of repairs makes goods hard or uneconomic to fix, such as glued-in components or overpriced spare parts.
Programmed obsolescence deliberately disables a working product, such as ink cartridge chips that stop use while ink remains.

definition.text: When products still work but seem out of date because styles change, so buyers replace them.

facts.text: It arises from consumer perception rather than from a designer's plan.
Fashion goods such as clothing go through a 'fashion cycle' that manufacturers ride with new designs while old ones still work.

definition.text: Using the Earth's limited resources sustainably so that the same output or consumption is achieved with fewer resources and less environmental impact.

facts.text: Improvements can happen at the production, consumption and end-of-life stages of a product.
Its measures and aims closely resemble those of resource productivity, resource intensity and eco-efficiency.
A key tool is measuring resource use, such as carbon, water and land footprints, and finding the 'hot spots' where most is used or most can be saved.
A resource-efficient Europe was one of seven flagship initiatives of the EU's Europe 2020 strategy.
The European Commission noted trade-offs: green vehicles cut fossil fuel use but add pressure on electricity, rare-earth elements and lithium.

definition.text: The amount of a resource, such as water, energy or materials, needed to produce, process and dispose of one unit of a good or service.

facts.text: Nationally it can be calculated as units of resource used per unit of GDP.
High resource intensity means a high price or environmental cost of turning resources into GDP.
It is the mirror image of resource productivity: resource use per unit of outcome rather than outcome per unit of resource; the goal is to minimize intensity and maximize productivity.
The OECD and UNEP use resource intensity indicators to track progress in decoupling growth from environmental damage.

definition.text: The amount of a good or service obtained for each unit of resource used.

facts.text: It can be expressed as money earned per unit of resource, such as 'crop per drop' of irrigation water.
With resource intensity, it is a key measure of attempts to decouple resource use from environmental degradation.
Research by Joachim Spangenberg suggests a transition focused on resource productivity gives higher growth than business as usual while easing environmental pressure.

definition.text: Established ways of moving toward sustainability, classically the three strategies of sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.

facts.text: Joseph Huber introduced the original triad of sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.
Sufficiency cuts consumption and production without threatening human needs and is linked to degrowth.
Efficiency cuts resource use, energy or pollution per unit of output within existing systems and has an affinity with green growth.
Consistency shifts to industrial metabolisms more in tune with nature's, such as renewable energy and circular design, and is rooted in industrial ecology.
Maria Sandberg distinguishes four types of sufficiency: absolute reduction, modal shifts, sharing and longer product life.

definition.text: Eric Hartmann's framework of ten sustainability strategies, five for future generations and five for people living today.

facts.text: The five intergenerational strategies add population reduction and regeneration expansion, such as reforestation, to sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.
The five intragenerational strategies are capability empowerment, equalization, eco-efficiency increase, impact expansion and population reduction.
Sustainability is achieved when everyone can meet fundamental needs while environmental impacts stay within safe limits.

definition.text: Using products and services in ways that keep their harm to the environment as small as possible.

facts.text: It covers decisions across the whole consumption cycle, from choosing and using products to disposing of them, to meet present needs with the least harm to environment, economy, society and culture.
It includes buying sustainable products, avoiding unsustainable ones, and extending product life through reuse and recycling.
Food systems cause about one third of global human-made greenhouse gas emissions, so shifting to more sustainable diets is part of it.
High-income people have larger energy footprints; the top 10% consume 56% of vehicle fuel, while the bottom half causes under 20% of energy footprints.
The 1992 Earth Summit recognized it as a concept in chapter 4 of Agenda 21.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 aims to 'ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns'.
Studies find that systemic change, not just individual ethical choices, is needed for a large effect on global warming.

title: Strong and weak sustainable consumption
article: Sustainable consumption#Strong and weak sustainable consumption

definition.text: A distinction between consumption that actively cuts environmental impact (strong) and consumption that fails to (weak).

facts.text: Strong sustainable consumption means choosing renewable, efficient goods and services, such as cycling or renewable energy, and reducing living space and consumption rates.
Weak sustainable consumption includes highly polluting habits such as frequent car use and buying non-biodegradable goods.
Research found people asked to cut energy use make only minimal sacrifices and fall short of strong sustainable consumption.

title: World3

definition.text: A system dynamics computer model simulating how population, industrial growth, food production and Earth's ecosystem limits interact.

facts.text: It was built for the Club of Rome study behind The Limits to Growth (1972) by project manager Dennis Meadows and 16 researchers, extending Jay Forrester's World2.
It assumes non-renewable resources are finite and get harder to extract, diverting a growing share of industrial capital to resource extraction.
Its reference run had world population peaking at seven billion in 2030 and persistent pollution peaking in 2035 at 11 times 1970s levels.
Donella Meadows had great confidence in its qualitative conclusions but mixed confidence in its numerical parameters, some of which were 'pure guesses'.
Vaclav Smil criticized lumping very different resources and pollutants into single variables as meaningless.
A study in Yale's Journal of Industrial Ecology found data broadly consistent with its 1972 projections.

contested_note: Critics question the model's lumped variables and guessed parameters, while validation studies find data tracking its projections.
